intent: Put a downstream context in a negotiated relationship with an upstream context that depends on it, so the supplier's backlog carries the customer's needs while the supplier keeps the final say.
problem: The downstream is dependent on the upstream and has legitimate input into what the upstream should build, but nothing in the process forces that input to be heard — so the downstream adapts to whatever the upstream happens to ship, and its own roadmap is hostage to someone else's priorities.
context: This is the customer-supplier half of the upstream/downstream pair; conformist is the same pair with negotiation removed. The defining move is organisational rather than technical: the downstream team's requirements get placed on the supplier's backlog and negotiated, with deprecation periods agreed in advance, while the supplier retains the final decision. It works when both contexts sit inside one organisation, or when the customer is the supplier's principal client. The technical half is whatever shape the negotiation produces — often an open host service when several customers share one supplier.
benefits: The downstream's needs enter the upstream's planning rather than being discovered afterwards.
Breaking changes come with agreed deprecation periods instead of surprises.
The supplier is motivated to keep the integration usable, because the customer matters.
The relationship can later be upgraded to an open host service without renegotiating from scratch.
Contract tests make the negotiated expectations executable.
tradeoffs: It requires ongoing negotiation discipline; without it this degrades into conformist with extra meetings.
The supplier can still decline, so the customer's roadmap is not guaranteed.
Multiple downstream customers negotiating separately turn the supplier into a bottleneck and force an open host service.
Negotiation has a real time cost in both organisations.
The relationship must be renegotiated whenever either side is reorganised or acquired.
quality_attributes_note: reliability 8 because negotiated deprecation periods remove surprise breaking changes. security 5 — the pattern says nothing about who is allowed to negotiate or consume.

participants.responsibility: Provides the model or service; makes the final call on priorities and design.
participants.notes: The customer's needs are on the supplier's backlog, not a command.

participants.responsibility: Depends on the supplier and has legitimate input into what is built.
participants.notes: Input is negotiated; the customer does not get unilateral control.

participants.responsibility: The ongoing process: prioritisation, deprecation windows, versioning policy.
participants.notes: This is the actual mechanism; without it there is only dependency.

participants.responsibility: Makes the negotiated expectations executable and fails both sides on drift.
participants.notes: Consumer-driven contract tests are the usual instrument.

use_cases: An internal platform team supplying an identity model to four product teams, with the teams' needs on the platform backlog.
Negotiated deprecation windows so a schema change does not break a downstream release.
A sole customer of a supplier, who therefore has real influence over the roadmap.
Consolidating several bespoke integrations into one open host service as customer numbers grow.
avoid_when: The supplier is external and does not negotiate — use conformist or an anti-corruption layer.
The supplier has many equal customers and no capacity to negotiate individually — build an open host service and a published language.
The customer has no real business leverage and the relationship would only ever be ceremonial.
The two contexts are really one; the negotiation is theatre.
pitfalls: Calling it a partnership when one side simply does what it is told.
Recording customer requests in the supplier backlog with no commitment attached, so nothing ever happens.
Negotiating once at the start and never again, until the first breaking change.
Several customers each negotiating bespoke integrations until the supplier is unmaintainable.
A dependency described as customer-supplier where the supplier could not possibly change its plan.

related_patterns_notes.conformist: Same upstream/downstream pair with negotiation removed; customer-supplier is strictly better when negotiation is actually available.
related_patterns_notes.open-host-service: What a supplier ends up building once it has many customers; the negotiated relationship is the one-to-one version.
related_patterns_notes.partnership: The symmetric alternative: where neither side is upstream, no negotiation structure is needed.
related_patterns_notes.consumer-driven-contract-test: Makes the negotiated expectations executable, which is what keeps the relationship honest.

anti_patterns: A backlog ticket labelled "customer request" with no negotiation attached.
Depending on an external vendor and describing the relationship as customer-supplier.
Negotiating deprecation periods verbally, so nobody downstream knows the rules.
One supplier accumulating bespoke per-customer integrations with no published interface.
Renaming conformism as customer-supplier to make an unavoidable dependency sound negotiated.
design_principles: In the customer/supplier relationship the two parties are encouraged to negotiate changes that affect each other, though the final word belongs to the supplier.
The downstream customer team can share concerns and expect the upstream supplier team to address them.
Customer-supplier is a parent-child relationship in which the downstream depends on the upstream and must adapt to its changes.
A shared kernel is appropriate only when the teams can coordinate; otherwise customer-supplier, conformist or an ACL.
With several downstream contexts, an open host service consolidates the separate customer-supplier relationships.
best_practices: Put the customer's needs on the supplier's backlog with an explicit mechanism, not as informal requests.
Agree deprecation periods in writing before the first breaking change, not during it.
Write consumer-driven contract tests so both sides can see when expectations drift.
Move to an open host service and a published language as soon as the supplier has more than a couple of customers.
Record the relationship and its terms on the context map, so the dependency is not folklore.
